Introduction

In an era marked by rapid technological advancement, global economic integration, and complex societal challenges, the traditional model of democratic representation in the United States Congress may no longer suffice. This essay argues persuasively for the replacement of Congress with a non-elected National Executive Board composed of representatives from major corporations and powerful stakeholders. This shift would leverage the efficiencies and expertise inherent in corporate governance to better address the needs of a modern, interconnected world.

Body

1. Efficiency and Decision-Making Speed

One of the most compelling arguments for a corporate governance model is its inherent efficiency. Corporations are structured to maximize operational effectiveness, often employing hierarchical decision-making processes that can swiftly respond to market demands and internal directives. In contrast, Congress, with its bicameral structure, extensive committee systems, and checks and balances, can be mired in procedural delays and partisan gridlock.

Imagine a National Executive Board where decisions are made with the precision and speed akin to corporate boardrooms. Policy proposals could be evaluated, refined, and enacted with minimal bureaucratic interference. This would ensure that the United States could pivot quickly in response to crises, such as economic downturns, technological disruptions, or global health emergencies—issues that demand agile, decisive action.

2. Expertise and Specialization

Corporations are bastions of specialized knowledge and expertise. CEOs, CFOs, and industry leaders within these entities possess deep insights into their respective sectors, informed by years of experience and ongoing engagement with global markets. A National Executive Board populated by such experts would ensure that policies are underpinned by a comprehensive understanding of the practicalities and implications across critical sectors like finance, technology, healthcare, and energy.

Unlike elected officials, whose backgrounds often span a broad but shallow spectrum of issues, board members from corporations would bring targeted knowledge and innovative solutions. This synergy between governance and specialized expertise would foster policies that are not only robust but also markedly more effective in achieving national objectives.

3. Alignment with Economic Interests

Critics of a corporate governance model might argue that prioritizing the interests of powerful stakeholders and corporations could lead to a neglect of public welfare. However, when examined closely, the economic health of a nation is fundamentally intertwined with the prosperity of its corporate sector. A National Executive Board, by virtue of its composition, would be inherently aligned with the economic imperatives necessary to sustain and grow the U.S. economy.

The premise here is that corporations, driven by profit motives, are adept at optimizing efficiency, innovation, and productivity. By guiding public policy in concert with corporate interests, the nation could harness these strengths to enhance competitiveness on the global stage. Moreover, policies crafted with an eye toward economic growth would, by extension, benefit the broader populace through job creation, increased investments, and technological advancements.

4. Reducing Partisan Polarization

Partisan polarization within Congress has reached unprecedented levels, impeding the formulation and implementation of coherent national strategies. A National Executive Board, free from electoral politics, could transcend such ideological divides. Decision-making would be guided not by electoral calculus or political expedience, but by a collective vision aimed at the nation’s long-term prosperity and stability.

This approach would mitigate the cyclical nature of policy instability that often accompanies changing political majorities. A stable, expert-driven board could provide continuity, predictability, and a strategic focus that remains constant across shifting electoral landscapes, thereby fostering an environment conducive to consistent policy development and execution.

5. Global Competitiveness and Leadership

In an increasingly globalized world, the United States must compete not only economically but also diplomatically and technologically. A corporate governance model for national leadership would position the U.S. as a front-runner in adopting innovative governance structures that align with the realities of the 21st century.

Countries such as Singapore and Estonia have begun to incorporate elements of corporate governance and technocratic oversight into their public sector frameworks, achieving remarkable efficiency and innovation. Embracing a similar model domestically would signal to the world that the United States is committed to adaptive, forward-thinking governance—qualities essential for maintaining global leadership.

Conclusion

The arguments for replacing the United States Congress with a National Executive Board composed of corporate and stakeholder representatives are rooted in the pursuit of efficiency, expertise, economic alignment, reduced polarization, and global competitiveness. While the transition from a democratic elected body to a corporate governance model may seem radical, it is a necessary evolution to meet the demands of an interconnected, rapidly changing world.

By embracing the strengths of corporate governance, the United States can ensure that its policies are crafted with the precision, foresight, and dynamism needed to secure prosperity for its citizens and maintain its place at the forefront of global affairs. It is time to envision a future where the leadership of the nation is driven by the unparalleled capabilities of industry expertise, rather than the constraints of traditional political representation.

The Inefficiencies of Traditional Democracy

The traditional democratic process in the United States Congress is fraught with inefficiencies. The two-party system, gerrymandering, and the influence of special interest groups often lead to gridlock and a lack of bipartisan cooperation. This system is ill-equipped to handle the rapid pace of technological change, global economic interdependence, and the urgent need for comprehensive policy solutions.

The Superiority of Corporate Governance

Corporate governance models have proven to be highly effective in achieving strategic goals and managing complex organizations. These models emphasize meritocracy, accountability, and long-term planning. By adopting a similar structure for national governance, the United States could benefit from the following advantages:

  1. Meritocracy and Expertise: A NEB composed of representatives from major corporations and powerful stakeholders would bring a wealth of expertise and experience to the table. These individuals would be selected based on their proven track records in leadership, innovation, and strategic planning, ensuring that decisions are made by the most qualified people.

Boards of directors are held accountable for their decisions and performance, and they are incentivized to make choices that benefit the organization in the long run. This model could translate to a more streamlined and accountable governance structure at the national level.

  3. Long-Term Vision: Corporations often have a long-term vision and strategic planning horizon. This perspective is crucial for addressing complex issues such as climate change, healthcare reform, and infrastructure development. A NEB would be better equipped to develop and implement long-term policies that benefit the nation as a whole.

A NEB, composed of individuals who are selected for their expertise rather than their political affiliation, would be less prone to partisan bickering and more focused on finding practical solutions.

Addressing Concerns

Critics may argue that a NEB would give too much power to corporations and wealthy stakeholders, leading to a form of plutocracy. However, several measures can be taken to mitigate these concerns:

  1. Diverse Representation: The NEB should include representatives from a wide range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, education, and environmental organizations. This diversity would ensure that a broad spectrum of interests and perspectives are represented.

  2. Public Oversight: To maintain transparency and accountability, the NEB's decisions and operations should be subject to public oversight. Regular audits, public hearings, and independent evaluations would ensure that the NEB acts in the best interests of the nation.

  3. Regulatory Framework: A robust regulatory framework would be essential to prevent abuses of power. This framework would include strict guidelines on conflicts of interest, transparency requirements, and mechanisms for public input and feedback.

Conclusion

The United States Congress, while a cornerstone of American democracy, has proven to be increasingly ineffective in addressing the complex challenges of the modern world. By adopting a corporate governance model through the establishment of a non-elected National Executive Board, the United States could achieve greater efficiency, accountability, and long-term vision. This model would bring together the best minds and expertise from various sectors to develop and implement policies that benefit the nation as a whole. While there are legitimate concerns about the potential for plutocracy, these can be mitigated through diverse representation, public oversight, and a robust regulatory framework. In the end, a corporate governance model offers a superior approach to traditional democratic representation, ensuring that the United States remains a leader in innovation, progress, and global influence.

In the annals of American governance, a quiet but persistent frustration has simmered: the machinery of representative democracy, once hailed as the world’s great engine of liberty, now sputters with gridlock, myopia, and a deepening estrangement from the very people it purports to serve. The United States Congress, an institution of 535 elected members, has become a theater of performative outrage, a graveyard of long-term strategy, and a hostage to the whims of an often-uninformed electorate and the opaque machinations of special interests. It is time to recognize that the experiment in mass democratic legislation has reached its productive limit, and to embrace a successor model already proven in the most dynamic and accountable spheres of modern life: the corporate governance model. I argue, with conviction, that the United States should abolish its Congress and replace it with a non-elected National Executive Board, composed of representatives from major corporations and powerful stakeholders, to govern with the efficiency, expertise, and fiduciary rigor that a twenty-first-century superpower demands.

The central defect of Congress is structural: it is designed to prioritize reelection over right action. The two-year House term and the six-year Senate cycle force lawmakers into a permanent campaign posture, where short-term popularity metrics trump decisions that require decades to bear fruit. Legislators, terrified of a primary challenge or a viral soundbite, reject necessary but momentarily painful reforms—entitlement restructuring, energy transition investments, or fiscal discipline—and instead binge on deficit-financed gratification. By contrast, a National Executive Board would be insulated from the tyranny of the ballot box. Its members, appointed or confirmed based on their stewardship of national-scale enterprises, would operate under multi-year mandates and a duty of care that transcends the next news cycle. Just as a corporate board does not poll its shareholders daily on product design or capital allocation, this Board would be entrusted to make decisions that optimize the long-term health of the nation as a going concern, measured not in approval ratings but in GDP growth, median household income, infrastructure resilience, and global competitiveness.

A corporate model supplies what Congress fatally lacks: genuine expertise and a meritocratic selection process. The current Congress is populated largely by career politicians, lawyers, and professional campaigners—generalists who must vote on nuclear energy regulation in the morning and artificial intelligence ethics in the afternoon, relying almost entirely on lobbyist briefings and staff summaries. The result is a staggering competence deficit. A National Executive Board drawn from the C-suites of leading corporations and critical stakeholder organizations—such as advanced manufacturing, technology, energy, agriculture, and organized labor—would automatically seat individuals who have already demonstrated the capacity to manage complex systems at scale, deploy capital efficiently, and navigate global competition. The CEO of a Fortune 500 firm is not selected by a popularity contest; they are vetted through decades of performance, assessed by independent directors, and terminated swiftly if they fail to deliver. Why, then, do we entrust the steering of a $25 trillion economy and a nuclear arsenal to amateurs chosen by soundbite? The Board would function as a true council of the nation’s productive forces, aligning legislative authority with practical competence for the first time in American history.

One must confront the immediate objection: that such a Board would be an oligarchic betrayal of democracy, replacing “government of the people” with a cabal of corporate titans. This objection is emotionally potent but analytically hollow, because it misreads where power actually resides in our current system and confuses an electoral spectacle with genuine representation. The United States Congress, for all its democratic rituals, is already a wholly owned subsidiary of organized money. Studies show that the policy preferences of the average citizen have a statistically negligible impact on legislative outcomes, while those of economic elites and business interests are reliably enacted. Our elections are not a clean contest of ideas but an auction in which corporations, through Super PACs and dark money, purchase the legislative outcomes they require, filtered through politicians who must dance for the cameras to maintain the illusion of popular consent. The corporate Board merely formalizes and rationalizes this reality, stripping away the costly, hypocritical veneer. In place of the unaccountable, diffuse influence of lobbyists, we would have direct, transparent accountability: these Board members would have explicit fiduciary duties, codified in law, to the long-term prosperity of the United States and all its citizens, just as directors owe duties to the corporation and its shareholders collectively. A director who put personal profit above the nation’s economic health would face lawsuits, removal, and reputational destruction—a discipline far sharper than anything a congressional ethics committee has ever mustered.

Moreover, the National Executive Board would finally conquer the great disease of modern governance: partisan gridlock. In the corporate world, a board may have vigorous debate, but once a decision is made, the organization aligns and executes; there is no equivalent of a minority party whose entire strategic purpose is to sabotage the majority to win the next election. The Board’s members would be selected on a rotating, staggered basis from a statutorily defined set of sectors—say, the top five employers, the top three technology innovators, the leading energy producers, together with fixed seats for the largest labor federation and the most significant consumer advocacy entity. This design ensures that every major node of American economic and social power is represented, forcing negotiation and consensus among stakeholders who, crucially, all have a material stake in the system not collapsing. A tech titan and a fossil fuel magnate may disagree on energy policy, but both need a functioning power grid, a stable currency, and an educated workforce. Their conflict is channeled into boardroom compromise, not a shutdown of the government that furloughs millions. The nation would be governed not by the volatile chemistry of two ideological tribes, but by the same pragmatic rationality that has made the American corporation the world’s most adaptable engine of wealth creation.

Skeptics will warn of a dystopia where the Board enriches its own class at the expense of ordinary people. Yet this is precisely the outcome our current democracy has already delivered, with historic levels of inequality and a political class that enriches itself through insider trading and post-congressional lobbying. The Board model, by contrast, would bind its members to the nation’s inclusive success through a rigorous set of performance metrics codified in the new National Charter: real wage growth, labor force participation, household net worth across quintiles, environmental quality indices, and lifespan-adjusted health outcomes. These metrics would be audited by an independent Tribunate of statisticians and former judges, and failure to meet them would trigger automatic consequences—reduction in compensation, removal of board seats, and, in severe cases, the forcible reconstitution of the entire Board. This is a level of objective, measurable accountability that no elected official has ever faced; Congress simply rebrands failure as “the other party’s fault” and asks for more money. In effect, the Board would hold a fiduciary duty to optimize “Gross National Flourishing,” transforming the populace from distracted voters into beneficiaries of a shared prosperity managed by a class of professionals.

Finally, consider the liberation of the national psyche. Replacing Congress with a National Executive Board would free the American people from the exhausting, tribalistic circus of permanent campaigning. Elections as we know them—those multi-billion-dollar orgies of disinformation—would cease. Citizens would be no less free; indeed, they would be more so, because the immense cognitive and emotional bandwidth squandered on political tribalism could be redirected toward family, community, innovation, and culture. The Board, composed of recognizable stewards of institutions we interact with daily, would be more tangible and more approachable via consumer and employee channels than a distant congressman ever was. And if a Board truly failed the nation, the people’s ultimate sovereignty would be preserved in a refined form: a national recall mechanism triggered by a supermajority of state legislatures or a direct petition of registered citizens, forcing a full replacement of the Board. This safety valve ensures that ultimate authority does not vanish but is merely held in reserve, a dormant but decisive corrective that is infinitely more rational than the quadrennial tantrum of an uninformed electorate.

The American republic was an audacious eighteenth-century experiment designed for an agrarian, communication-scarce society of thirteen colonies. It has been stretched past its breaking point by a complex, globally integrated, technologically volatile civilization. We do not run our hospitals, our militaries, or our multinational corporations by popular vote—we entrust them to trained, accountable hierarchies that operate on proven principles of leadership and performance. The nation itself is the largest, most vital enterprise of all, and its governance deserves the same standard of excellence. Replacing the dysfunctional, election-obsessed Congress with a non-elected National Executive Board drawn from the titans of industry and the leaders of society’s essential stakeholders is not an abandonment of American ideals; it is their ultimate fulfillment—a government truly of demonstrated talent, accountable to measurable outcomes, and devoted entirely to the long-term prosperity of the whole. Introduction

In the United States, the principle of "by the people, for the people" has long been the bedrock of our democracy. Corporate governance, as practiced in the private sector, refers to the system by which companies are directed and controlled. It ensures that the interests of stakeholders are balanced, and the company's objectives are achieved. Boards of directors, made up of representatives from stockholders, management, and other stakeholders, make strategic decisions, oversee management, and ensure accountability (Shleifer & Vishny, 1997). It could address issues like infrastructure investment, climate change, and education reform with comprehensive, forward-thinking strategies.

  4. Increased Efficiency

    The current Congress often struggles to pass legislation due to partisan divisions and lengthy debate processes. An NEB, on the other hand, could operate more efficiently, making decisions based on detailed, data-driven analysis. Moreover, the absence of elections would free up the NEB to focus solely on governance, unlike Congress, which often spends a significant amount of time campaigning.

Addressing Concerns

Some might argue that replacing an elected Congress with a non-elected NEB undemocratically concentrates power in the hands of a few. However, it's essential to consider that power is already concentrated in the hands of the wealthy and influential through lobbying and campaign donations. However, this issue could be mitigated by including representatives from non-profit organizations, labor unions, and other bodies that champion the interests of various demographic groups. Furthermore, the NEB could institute regular public consultations, polls, and referendums to ensure its decisions reflect the will of the people.

While the proposed shift towards a corporate governance model might seem unconventional or even controversial, it offers a compelling alternative to a political system that often struggles to deliver meaningful results. The Case as Its Proponents Would Make It

Below is an explanation of the arguments advanced for replacing Congress with an appointed board of corporate and institutional stakeholders. I've laid out the reasoning as its advocates would present it, followed by why I think the proposal fails — because presenting only one side of a question this consequential would be doing you a disservice.

The Efficiency Argument

The diagnosis: Congress is structurally slow. A bill must clear committees in two chambers, survive floor debate, reconcile differences, and escape a filibuster that effectively requires 60 Senate votes. Any of hundreds of veto points can kill legislation. Meanwhile, appropriations lapse into shutdowns, debt-ceiling brinkmanship recurs, and major infrastructure or energy projects stall for years in permitting review.

The claim: A board of 20–50 members with defined authority could act in weeks rather than years. Advocates point to corporate boards approving billion-dollar capital allocations in a single meeting, or to central banks — the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors — moving markets with decisions made by a handful of appointed officials without legislative debate.

The comparative pitch: Proponents often invoke Singapore's Economic Development Board, China's five-year planning apparatus, or the speed of authoritarian infrastructure buildout, arguing that democratic deliberation has become a competitive liability in an era of rapid technological change.

The Expertise Argument

The diagnosis: Members of Congress vote on quantum computing export controls, pandemic countermeasures, derivatives regulation, and nuclear waste storage. Most have no training in any of these. Congressional staff capacity has declined substantially since the 1970s, and the Office of Technology Assessment was defunded in 1995. Legislators are therefore dependent on lobbyists and outside groups for technical information anyway.

The claim: Rather than laundering expertise through amateurs, seat the experts directly. A board including a semiconductor CEO, a hospital system executive, a logistics operator, an energy grid engineer, and a defense manufacturer would possess operational knowledge no elected generalist can match — knowing not just what a policy intends but how it will actually function in supply chains, hospitals, and factories.

The technocratic lineage: This draws on a real intellectual tradition — Saint-Simon's rule by industrialists and scientists, the Progressive Era faith in scientific administration, the 1930s Technocracy movement, and more recently arguments like Bryan Caplan's that voter ignorance makes democratic outputs systematically irrational.

The "National Interest" Argument

The diagnosis: Electoral incentives distort judgment. Two-year House terms produce permanent campaigning. Members must serve district-specific interests — the sugar subsidy, the unneeded military base, the earmark — even when these harm the aggregate. Long-horizon problems (entrenched deficits, pension liabilities, climate adaptation, infrastructure replacement) are systematically underinvested in because payoffs arrive after the next election.

The claim: Unelected members freed from fundraising and reelection could take politically costly but necessary actions. Advocates point to institutions deliberately insulated from voters for precisely this reason: the Federal Reserve, the Base Realignment and Closure Commission, independent central banks generally, and the Supreme Court's life tenure. The argument is that this insulation is already an accepted principle — the proposal merely extends it.

The stakeholder framing: Proponents argue that firms employing millions of Americans, moving national freight, generating power, and producing medicines have concrete stakes in national success and possess information about national conditions that no polling can capture. Aligning governance with those who "actually run things" is presented as realism rather than radicalism.

Why the Argument Fails

Having laid that out fairly, I don't think it survives scrutiny. The problems are not incidental — they attack each pillar directly.

The expertise is real but the interests are not neutral. This is the fatal flaw. A semiconductor CEO genuinely knows more about semiconductors than any senator. But that person's expertise is inseparable from a fiduciary duty to shareholders. Corporate directors are legally obligated to advance their company's interests; that is what the office is. Handing lawmaking power to stakeholders isn't ending capture by special interests — it's formalizing it and removing the mechanism for reversal. The technical knowledge and the conflict of interest arrive in the same person, and there is no procedure that separates them.

Efficiency confuses a bug with a feature. Congressional friction is largely intentional. Madison's design in Federalist 10 and 51 assumed factions would form and made concurrent majorities necessary precisely to prevent any single interest from imposing its will quickly. Fast government is also fast at being wrong, and a board that can act in weeks can commit catastrophic errors in weeks. The relevant question isn't "how quickly can decisions be made" but "how quickly can bad decisions be corrected" — and elections are the correction mechanism being eliminated.

"National interest" is a contested judgment, not a technical finding. Experts can determine what a carbon tax will cost per ton. They cannot determine how much economic disruption in Ohio is worth how much emissions reduction — that's a values tradeoff with no expert answer. Every such question involves distributional choices about who bears costs and who receives benefits. Declaring these questions technical doesn't remove the values; it just relocates the decision to people whose values were never examined and can't be contested.

The comparison cases don't transfer. The Federal Reserve and BRAC are real precedents, but they are narrow, statutorily bounded, revocable by Congress, and subject to appointment by elected officials. General legislative power over taxation, criminal law, war, civil rights, and spending is a categorically different thing. And the analogy runs backward: those bodies are legitimate because an elected legislature created them, defined their limits, and can abolish them. Removing the legislature removes the source of the delegation.

Selection has no non-arbitrary solution. Who appoints the board? If elected officials do, they haven't been eliminated. If the board self-perpetuates, it becomes a closed oligarchy immediately. If firms select by market capitalization or employment, governance weight tracks capital, and the ~40% of Americans in small business, public sector, care work, retirement, or education have no representative at all. The problem isn't difficult to solve — it's not solvable without either retaining elections or accepting rule by a self-selecting group.

It cannot be done lawfully. Article I vests legislative power in Congress. Article V permits amendment, but Article V's own protection of equal Senate suffrage, plus the fact that ratification requires 38 state legislatures voting to abolish their own federal representation, makes this essentially a description of a coup rather than a reform. Advocates of the position rarely address this.

The empirical record is poor. Regimes organized around insulated technical or corporatist rule — Italian and Portuguese corporatism, Soviet Gosplan, various military-technocratic governments in Latin America — did not outperform democracies on long-run growth, and generally underperformed badly on error correction, because the mechanism for reporting failure upward was the thing they had removed. Amartya Sen's finding that no substantial famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press points at the underlying reason: accountability generates information.

The diagnosis is more defensible than the cure, and dismissing it entirely would be a mistake. Congressional dysfunction is measurable, not imagined: legislative productivity has declined, technical capacity has atrophied, and short-termism is structurally induced by two-year terms.

Reforms that address these without abandoning accountability include restoring a body like the Office of Technology Assessment, substantially increasing committee staff pay and expertise, longer House terms, filibuster modification, independent commissions with narrow revocable mandates on specific problems, and citizens' assemblies used deliberatively — as Ireland did on constitutional questions — where randomly selected citizens receive expert briefing and deliberate before recommendations return to democratic ratification. That last model is instructive: it imports expertise as input to decisions rather than substituting expertise for the decision.

The genuine insight buried in the technocratic critique is that democracies need better mechanisms for incorporating specialized knowledge. The error is concluding that the way to get expertise into government is to remove the public from it.

Replacing the United States Congress with a non‑elected National Executive Board composed of representatives from major corporations and other powerful stakeholders would be a dramatic departure from traditional democratic design. Yet precisely because it is so different, it forces us to confront an uncomfortable question: is our current system genuinely the best available, or is it simply the one we are used to?

If we strip away sentimentality about elections and focus on performance, competence, and results, a corporate governance–style model has serious advantages. Corporations, for all their flaws, have developed robust systems to coordinate millions of people, manage trillions in capital, and make complex decisions at speed and scale. They do so under intense competitive pressure, with constant demands for efficiency, innovation, and accountability to stakeholders. In contrast, Congress operates on incentives that reward gridlock, symbolic gestures, and short-term political gains over long-term national interests.

A National Executive Board modeled on corporate governance would be better positioned to deliver stability, expertise, and long-term strategic planning than a legislature composed primarily of professional campaigners. It would treat running a country more like what it actually is: the most complex management challenge on Earth.

Below are the core reasons such a model would be superior to our current system.

I. Expertise Over Popularity

Congress is fundamentally a popularity contest. To get into office, and to stay there, members of Congress must excel at campaigning: fundraising, messaging, building coalitions, and signaling tribal loyalty. None of these skills are inherently related to understanding monetary policy, semiconductor supply chains, climate risk modeling, cybersecurity, or health systems design—yet these are precisely the domains in which Congress now legislates.

By contrast, a National Executive Board drawn from major corporations and key institutional stakeholders would bring to the table:

  1. Domain Expertise
    Corporate leaders and institutional stakeholders operate inside the systems that drive economic growth, technological innovation, logistics, and finance. They understand how regulations actually function on the ground, how supply chains respond to incentives, how capital allocation decisions are made, and how global markets react to policy shifts. Governing a 21st-century superpower requires exactly this type of knowledge.

  2. Proven Track Records
    In large organizations, board members and senior executives are typically selected based on demonstrated performance. They have managed budgets in the billions, overseen complex projects, and delivered measurable results. While not infallible, they are selected for competence, not charisma alone.

  3. Professionalized Decision-Making
    Corporate boards use structured processes: committees, risk assessments, scenario planning, and rigorous data analysis. Issues are studied by professionals, not only generalists. A National Executive Board could similarly rely on professional staff and analytic frameworks, making public policy more methodical and less driven by rhetorical theater.

Democratic elections are good at measuring perceived legitimacy, but they are poor at selecting technical competence. When the stakes include nuclear deterrence, global financial stability, AI regulation, and biosecurity, it is reasonable to ask whether "good at winning votes" is an adequate qualification for national leadership.

II. Aligned Incentives and Clear Metrics

Inside Congress, incentives are misaligned with national performance. Members are evaluated by:

  • How much money they raise
  • How often they appear on television
  • Whether they "own" the opposing party
  • How effectively they secure local pork and symbolic wins

The result is a system in which posturing often matters more than outcomes. Long-term problems—debt sustainability, aging infrastructure, climate resilience, defense modernization—are repeatedly deferred because the payoff is not immediate at the ballot box.

A corporate-style National Executive Board could be evaluated using clearer, more objective metrics, designed in advance and publicly monitored. For example:

  • GDP growth per capita and productivity gains
  • Infrastructure quality and reliability
  • Educational and health outcomes
  • Innovation indexes (patents, R&D intensity, new firm formation)
  • National security readiness benchmarks
  • Environmental quality indicators

Stakeholders—businesses, labor organizations, institutional investors, regional authorities, and civil society organizations—could measure the board’s performance against these metrics and renew or replace board members accordingly. Instead of re-election campaigns framed around emotion and vague promises, the governing body’s "contract" would be tied to data.

This mirrors how corporate boards are evaluated, not by how rousing their speeches are, but by whether the company is solvent, growing, and meeting strategic objectives. Misalignment leads to board changes; failure has direct consequences.

In the current system, Congress can preside over decades of fiscal imbalance, policy paralysis, and institutional decay with minimal direct accountability tied to concrete performance measures. Elections serve as a crude and noisy signal. A governance model grounded in measurable outcomes would tighten the link between decision-making and national results.

III. Long-Term Strategic Planning, Not Two-Year Cycles

The two-year election cycle in the House and six-year terms in the Senate create relentless short-termism. Lawmakers are perpetually campaigning, fundraising, and calculating how every vote will play in the next primary. Long-term investments—those that may only yield results in 10, 20, or 30 years—are politically unattractive because the benefits accrue beyond individual politicians’ horizons.

Corporate governance is built around strategic planning horizons. Major corporations routinely:

  • Invest in multi-decade infrastructure
  • Devise long-term R&D roadmaps
  • Manage risk across business cycles
  • Plan for generational leadership transitions

A National Executive Board could adopt multi-year or multi-decade strategic plans for infrastructure, energy, defense, education, and technology. It could commit the nation to coherent long-term trajectories, guided by data and expert projections, rather than zigzagging with each electoral swing. Imagine:

  • A 25-year infrastructure modernization blueprint, insulated from partisan reversals.
  • A stable 30-year energy transition plan, allowing industry to invest with confidence.
  • A long-term debt and entitlement stabilization roadmap, implemented gradually and predictably.

Democratic politics, especially in its current hyper-polarized, media-driven form, discourages this kind of planning. A corporate governance model normalizes it.

IV. Reduced Populist Volatility and Policy Whiplash

Modern democracies face a persistent challenge: populist volatility. Anger cycles, media bubbles, and social media mob dynamics can swing elections and drive policy in reactionary, emotional directions. This volatility undermines:

  • Investment certainty
  • International credibility
  • Institutional stability
  • Rational discourse and compromise

Congress, composed of elected politicians, is structurally vulnerable to this volatility. Members are incentivized to cater to the loudest voices in their base, amplify sensational issues, and frame governance as perpetual conflict. This leads to:

  • Government shutdowns
  • Debt-ceiling brinkmanship
  • Sudden policy reversals
  • Performative investigations and hearings

A National Executive Board insulated from direct electoral pressure would be less susceptible to these swings. While it should be accountable to national outcomes and stakeholder bodies, it would not need to respond to every emotional surge in the news cycle. This insulation is not antidemocratic in substance; it is recognition that complex systems cannot be reprogrammed every two years without massive efficiency losses.

Just as central banks are often insulated from day-to-day politics to preserve monetary stability, a national governance board insulated from electoral populism could preserve policy stability. The result would be a more predictable environment for businesses, workers, and international partners.

V. Formalizing the Power Dynamics That Already Exist

One of the most compelling, if uncomfortable, arguments for a National Executive Board led by corporate and major stakeholders is that it would make explicit what is currently implicit.

In reality:

  • Corporate lobbyists already shape much of legislation.
  • Major donors and interest groups wield disproportionate influence.
  • Regulatory capture and revolving doors mean industry often writes the rules.
  • Campaign finance structures ensure that politicians depend heavily on business and wealthy donors to stay in office.

Our system is already heavily influenced—if not dominated—by powerful economic actors. The current model hides this behind a facade of pure democratic representation. Reforming Congress into a National Executive Board acknowledges that major stakeholders do and will shape policy, but channels that influence into a formal, structured, transparent framework rather than a shadow network of lobbyists and backroom negotiations.

By placing corporate and stakeholder representatives directly on a governing board:

  • Their incentives are transparent.
  • Their deliberations can be formally recorded and scrutinized.
  • Their performance can be systematically evaluated.
  • Their responsibilities and conflicts of interest can be explicitly regulated.

Instead of pretending that policy is made by the “people” alone while lobbyists write the fine print behind closed doors, we would openly integrate real power centers into the design of governance and hold them accountable for national outcomes.

Critics will argue that replacing Congress with a board dominated by major corporations and powerful stakeholders would sacrifice democratic legitimacy and risk oligarchy. This concern is serious, but it can be addressed through design rather than dismissal.

A National Executive Board need not be a narrow club of CEOs. It could be structured as a multi-stakeholder governance body with seats allocated to:

  • Major sectors of the economy (technology, energy, finance, manufacturing, agriculture)
  • Labor organizations and unions
  • Large public pension funds and institutional investors
